extracted.intended_audience: Authors, peer reviewers, editors, publishers, and journal owners involved in medical/biomedical journal publishing
extracted.subtask_description: Comprehensive recommendations for the conduct, reporting, editing, and publication of scholarly work in medical journals, covering authorship, conflicts of interest, peer review, editorial responsibilities, manuscript preparation, research participant protection, and use of AI in publishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship criteria (ICMJE four criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship should be based on all four criteria: (1) substantial contributions to conception/design or acquisition/analysis/interpretation of data; AND (2) drafting the work or critical revision for important intellectual content; AND (3) final approval of the version to be published; AND (4) agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work with assurance that questions about accuracy or integrity will be investigated and resolved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All persons designated as authors should meet all four criteria, and all who meet the criteria should be identified as authors. Those who meet only some criteria should be acknowledged. Individuals who meet criterion #1 should be given the opportunity to meet criteria #2 and #3. Authors should be able to identify which co-authors are responsible for specific parts of the work and have confidence in co-authors' integrity. The group should decide authorship early for large multi-author groups; journals are not responsible for arbitrating authorship disputes—institutions should investigate unresolved disagreements. Do not use authorship criteria to deny opportunity to participate in drafting/reviewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corresponding author responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The corresponding author takes primary responsibility for communication with the journal during submission, peer-review, and publication, and typically ensures administrative requirements (authorship details, ethics approvals, trial registration, disclosures) are completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corresponding author should be available throughout submission and after publication to respond to editorial queries and cooperate with requests for data or additional information. Duties may be delegated but editors are encouraged to send correspondence to all listed authors. For group-authored works, the corresponding author should specify group name and identify individuals who can take credit and responsibility. If authors request post-submission/byline changes, editors should seek explanation and signed agreement from all authors and the person to be added/removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-author contributors and acknowledgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributors who do not meet all four authorship criteria should not be listed as authors but should be acknowledged with their specific contributions described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of activities that alone do not qualify for authorship: acquisition of funding, general supervision, administrative support, writing assistance, technical/language editing, and proofreading. Acknowledged individuals' contributions should be specified (e.g., 'collected data,' 'provided clinical care'). Editors should require written permission from acknowledged individuals because acknowledgment may imply endorsement. Use of AI for writing assistance should be reported in the acknowledgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of financial and non-financial relationships and activities (conflicts of interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: All participants (authors, peer reviewers, editors, editorial board members) must consider and disclose relationships and activities that might bias or appear to bias their roles in planning, implementing, reviewing, editing, and publishing scientific work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ICMJE Disclosure Form to standardize disclosures. Disclose financial relationships (employment, consultancy, stock, honoraria, patents, paid testimony) and non-financial interests (personal relationships, academic competition, intellectual beliefs) that may create perceived or actual conflicts. Purposeful failure to report specified relationships is misconduct. Editors should publish their own disclosure statements and those of staff. Reviewers and editors should recuse themselves if conflicts exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting relationships and activities in publications (funding, sponsor role, data access)
rubrics_metrics.description: Articles should include statements or supporting documents declaring authors’ relationships and activities; sources of support for the work including sponsor names and the sponsor's role; and whether authors had access to the study data (nature, extent, ongoing access).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding statements should distinguish direct support for the work from support for an individual's time or general institutional support. Editors may request signed statements from authors in studies sponsored by entities with proprietary/financial interests (e.g., 'I had full access to all of the data...'). Disclosures extend beyond direct support for the reported work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors' responsibility to avoid predatory/pseudo-journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must evaluate the integrity, history, practices, and reputation of journals before submitting and avoid entities that accept/publish almost all submissions while claiming peer review and charging fees after acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should consult guidance (WAME, COPE, ICMJE) and seek mentors' advice. Avoid citing articles from predatory/pseudo-journals. Predatory journals may falsely claim membership in organizations; check official member lists on icmje.org.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of manuscripts and reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts submitted to journals are privileged, confidential communications and editors, reviewers, and editorial staff must keep manuscript details strictly confidential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors must not share manuscript status, content, reviewer criticism, or other details beyond authors and reviewers. Reviewers must keep manuscripts confidential, not appropriate ideas, and destroy/delete copies after review. Using AI systems that compromise confidentiality (e.g., uploading a manuscript to external AI where confidentiality cannot be assured) is prohibited without explicit permission. Requests for manuscripts for legal proceedings should be politely refused where possible. When manuscripts are rejected, journals should usually delete copies unless retention is required by regulations; published papers' submission materials should be kept for at least three years or longer as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and responsiveness of editorial process
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should ensure timely processing of manuscripts and respond to author queries; if not proceeding they should reject quickly; planned delays should be negotiated with authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should respond promptly to status requests and treat good-faith withdrawal requests as withdrawn even if confirmation isn't received. Editors should attempt to publish accepted manuscripts in a timely manner. Journals should publish clear descriptions of their processes and timeframes where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for peer review processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals must have systems to select appropriate reviewers, ensure reviewers have access to relevant materials, and interpret reviewer comments in context of declared relationships and activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may vary in number/type of reviewers and openness of review; they should publish transparent descriptions of their peer-review process. Reviewers should be notified of final decisions and acknowledged. Editors are encouraged to share reviewers’ comments with co-reviewers. Editors should consider reviewing research protocols, statistical analysis plans, and project-specific contracts; may require or encourage public posting of these documents. Journals should state their requirements for independent data analysis and data availability and preserve primary data/analytic procedures for at least 10 years (encourage repositories). Provide mechanisms for post-publication comments, questions, and criticisms; authors are expected to cooperate with post-publication inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer responsibilities and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must maintain confidentiality, declare conflicts of interest, recuse themselves if biased, respond promptly, and provide constructive, honest, and polite comments; they must not appropriate authors' ideas or retain manuscripts for personal use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers seeking assistance (e.g., trainee) must acknowledge contributors in comments to the editor. Reviewers must request permission before using AI tools for reviews and should not upload manuscripts to AI where confidentiality cannot be assured. Reviewers should be mindful that AI outputs can be incorrect, incomplete, or biased and must ensure validity of any AI-assisted content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial integrity and decision-making
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial decisions should be based on relevance, originality, quality, and contribution to evidence; decisions must not be influenced by commercial interests, personal relationships, agendas, or whether results are negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should consider negative or inconclusive studies for publication; journals should state appeals processes and have systems to respond to appeals and complaints. Editors may reject articles at any time, including post-acceptance, if integrity concerns arise. Editors should ensure decisions are not unduly affected by journal owners' commercial goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity, inclusion, and respectful representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should engage a broad and diverse array of authors, reviewers, editorial staff, and readers; when publishing images, avoid depictions that perpetuate bias or stereotypes or show individuals in vulnerability unless necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider dignity, equality, and solidarity; evaluate whether images are necessary for understanding. Seek to improve academic culture via diverse engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of journal and article metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not over-emphasize journal impact factor as a single measure of quality; provide a range of article and journal metrics relevant to readers and authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICMJE recommends reducing reliance on impact factor for assessing research, journals, or individual researchers (hiring, promotion, tenure). Journals should present multiple relevant metrics instead of a single proxy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal owners, governance, and editorial freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners and editors have distinct responsibilities; owners should appoint/dismiss editors only for substantial reasons and provide clear contracts; editors-in-chief should have full authority over editorial content and timing (editorial freedom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dismissals should be for substantial reasons (e.g., misconduct, inadequate performance) and assessed by independent panels. Owners should not interfere with article selection, scheduling, or editing. Editors should have direct access to highest ownership level, have final say on advertisements/supplement content, and be supported with insurance/legal advice. Establish independent, diverse editorial advisory boards to uphold policy. Editors and organizations should defend editorial freedom publicly when transgressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of research participants and ethics approvals
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators must ensure planning, conduct, and reporting of human research conform to the Helsinki Declaration and obtain approval from independent local/regional/national review bodies; be prepared to provide documentation to editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If researchers deviated from Helsinki, authors must explain rationale and show explicit approval for doubtful aspects. Approval by a review body doesn't preclude editor judgment about appropriateness. Patients' privacy must not be violated without informed consent; identifying details should not be published unless essential and written informed consent (showing the manuscript to the patient) is obtained and archived as required by regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript preparation: general principles and reporting guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should follow general principles for clear, accurate, reproducible reporting and authors should consult and follow study-specific reporting guidelines (e.g., CONSORT for randomized trials).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICMJE guidance is intended to be used along with individual journal 'Instructions for Authors' and reporting checklists. Some guidance is reiterated across sections to enable self-contained consultation. Authors should prepare standard manuscript sections (title page, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion, references, tables, figures) and follow journal-specific formatting and submission requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript sections: title page, abstract, introduction, methods, results, discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should include standard sections with content appropriate to each (title page details, structured abstract where required, clear introduction stating objectives, detailed methods including participant selection/data collection/statistics, results with appropriate reporting, and discussion that interprets results and states limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods should include selection and description of participants, measurements, and statistical methods; state primary/secondary outcomes and sample-size considerations. Results should present data clearly without duplication from tables/figures. Discussion should contextualize findings, state limitations, and avoid overstating conclusions; propose new hypotheses clearly labeled as such.

rubrics_metrics.name: References: content, accuracy, format, and ethical citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide direct references to original research when possible; cite published articles rather than abstracts; when citing preprints, label them as preprints; avoid citing predatory journals; verify references and avoid citing retracted work except to discuss retraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use PubMed/MEDLINE as authoritative source for retractions. References should be numbered consecutively as first mentioned; follow NLM 'Citing Medicine' and journal-specific style. Reference lists should balance comprehensiveness with concision; persistent identifiers for datasets should be included. Personal communications should be used sparingly and require written permission and confirmation of accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables: preparation and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables should capture information concisely, be numbered consecutively in order cited, have short self-explanatory titles, and include explanatory footnotes (not headings) and clear column headings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place explanatory matter in footnotes, explain nonstandard abbreviations there, identify statistical measures (SD, SE), and ensure each table is cited in text. Prepare tables so they can be imported to journal software when possible. If using previously published data, obtain permission. Extensive backup tables may be published online or deposited in repositories; state availability in the manuscript and submit them for peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures and illustrations: quality, legends, permissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit high-quality digital images suitable for print; number figures consecutively in order cited; provide legends on a separate page; include scale markers for photomicrographs; ensure labels remain legible when reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For clinical/radiologic images, submit high-resolution files; before-and-after images should have consistent lighting; original blot photographs may be required. If a figure was published previously, acknowledge source and provide written permission from copyright holder. Put detailed explanations in legends not on images; identify and explain symbols/arrows/letters used in figures. Editors may redraw figures but many do not, so prepare carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Units of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Report length, height, weight, volume in metric units (meter, kilogram, liter) or decimal multiples; temperatures in degrees Celsius and blood pressures in mm Hg unless otherwise required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report laboratory measures in both local and SI units as journals vary; editors may request alternative or non-SI units. Drug concentrations may be reported in SI or mass units with alternatives provided in parentheses where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations and symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Use only standard abbreviations and avoid nonstandard ones; avoid abbreviations in the title; define abbreviations on first mention (spelled-out then abbreviation in parentheses) unless the abbreviation is a standard unit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit use of abbreviations to improve readability. Explain nonstandard abbreviations in table footnotes or figure legends as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover letter and submission documentation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts should be accompanied by a cover letter or submission form including statements about redundant/related submissions, conflicts of interest, authorship confirmation, contact information for responsible author, prior submission history, and permissions to reproduce materials or identify persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include copies of related material that might be regarded as redundant publication and reference them specifically; provide funding/conflict statements if not in manuscript; state that all authors have read and approved the manuscript and meet authorship requirements (if contribution declarations not required); provide contact info for author responsible for revisions and proofs. Include presubmission checklists or reporting checklists when required by journal, and include permissions for previously published material or patient-identifiable information. If manuscript was previously submitted elsewhere, include prior editor/reviewer comments and authors' responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AI/LLM tools in publishing — overarching principles
rubrics_metrics.description: AI/LLM tools may be used but humans remain ultimately responsible for accuracy, transparency, confidentiality, and attribution. AI tools cannot be listed as authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users must disclose use of AI tools (which tool and purpose) at submission and in the manuscript where applicable (e.g., acknowledgments, methods). AI-generated content must be reviewed and edited by humans; referencing AI-generated material as a primary source is unacceptable. Ensure no plagiarism in AI-produced text/images and provide appropriate attribution for quoted material. Nondisclosure of AI use may lead to corrective action or be considered misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AI by reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must adhere to the journal's AI policy and request permission before using AI to facilitate a review; they must not upload submitted manuscripts into AI systems where confidentiality cannot be assured without journal permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reviewers use AI, they should disclose its use to the journal and ensure AI-assisted content is valid, accurate, and unbiased. Maintain confidentiality; avoid AI use that risks exposing manuscript content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' responsibilities regarding AI use
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should ensure responsible use of AI by querying authors about AI use, requiring disclosure, preventing AI-related confidentiality breaches, and having explicit journal policies on AI use in preparation, editing, and review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should distinguish acceptable uses (e.g., spell-check/grammar) from problematic uses (content generation) and require authors to check accuracy of AI-generated content. Editors and reviewers should not upload manuscripts to AI where confidentiality cannot be assured without authors’ explicit permission. If journals use AI in production (e.g., copy-editing) or for ancillary content, they should disclose this to authors. Editors are responsible for the accuracy of AI-assisted content published under the journal brand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data preservation, accessibility, and clinical trials registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators have a duty to maintain primary data and analytic procedures underpinning published results for at least 10 years and should deposit data in repositories where feasible; clinical trials should be registered, and authors should state authors' data access and data sharing plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals may require public posting of protocols, statistical analysis plans, or independent statistical review. Journals should publish their requirements for data analysis and post-publication data availability. Statements about data access should explain the nature and extent of access (ongoing or not).
